title: [Bug]: Five measured places the CLI spends time and tokens the work does not need: serial tool calls, uncached full-context calls and 70 s compactions, 12 s headless overhead, summary store rewritten every 1.5 s, build-time CPU instruction choice

labels.name: subtype:windows
labels.description: Windows specific issues (e.g., login links, PowerShell statusline)

labels.name: feedback
labels.description: Feedback on agy cli (other than performance issues etc)

body:
### Antigravity CLI Version

1.4.2 (Windows 11 Pro 10.0.26340), Hub 2.24. Measurements taken on 18–19 October 2026 on one machine. Every number below comes with the command or the log field that produced it, so each one can be re-run. Where I could only observe a correlation and not a cause, I say so.

### Environment

- Machine: AMD Ryzen 7 5800H (8 cores / 16 threads), 32 GB RAM, Windows 11 Pro 10.0.26340, system drive 464 GB.
- Headless invocation used for the long runs: `agy -p "<prompt>" --model gemini-4-argon-high --sandbox --output-format stream-json`, resumed with `agy -c -p`.
- The 15 stream-json logs behind sections 1–2 cover two multi-agent Three.js builds (orchestrator plus `invoke_subagent` module agents, `schedule` polling), 1,279 model calls in total. The one-minute repros in sections 1 and 3 use `gemini-3.8-flash-low` so anyone can run them cheaply.
- A Gravitas plugin (rules + skills) is installed, which is where the 32.6k-token prefix in section 3 comes from; the overhead numbers are the same with the prefix cached.

### Summary

Five places where the CLI spends time or tokens that the work does not need. They are not five bugs to patch one by one; each is a design choice in the harness, and each section ends with the design I would ask for instead of a workaround.

| # | What | Measured | Root-cause design |
|---|------|----------|-------------------|
| 1 | Tool calls issued together in one model step run one after another | three 6-s sleeps finish at 7.8 / 14.8 / 22.0 s | effect-typed scheduler |
| 2 | Full-context cache misses and compaction resets | 17 calls carry 31 % of all uncached input tokens; 22 compactions, median 70 s, cost not reported | byte-stable prefix contract, miss telemetry, cache-aware compaction |
| 3 | Fixed client overhead per headless call | 11.3–12.2 s on five runs | resident supervisor, thin client |
| 4 | Summary store serialised whole, continuously | 943 KB file rewritten 27 times in 90 s | journal plus debounce |
| 5 | CPU instruction use fixed at build time | `SIGILL` on CPUs without `pclmul` (#378) | runtime dispatch, the way Go's own crypto does it |

---

### 1. Tool calls issued together in one model step are executed serially

Repro, about one minute, any model:

```text
agy -p "In a single step, call run_command three times, in parallel, each with exactly this PowerShell command: Start-Sleep -Seconds 6; Get-Date -Format HH:mm:ss.fff . Do not wait for one before starting the next. When all three have returned, reply with only the three timestamps on one line." --model gemini-3.8-flash-low --sandbox --output-format stream-json
```

The model issues all three calls in one step. The stream-json shows them completing one after another:

```text
step 1 agent_response  4.2 s
step 2 tool run_command  7.8 s
step 3 tool run_command 14.8 s   (cumulative)
step 4 tool run_command 22.0 s
step 5 agent_response  4.4 s
result: "15:08:19.626 15:08:26.814 15:08:34.072"   duration_seconds 31.9
```

Yesterday's run of the same prompt gave 8.3 / 15.3 / 22.5 s and 32.3 s. The timestamps are 7.2 s apart; the turn would be about 17 s with the three commands running concurrently. In one orchestrated build conversation (five headless legs), 104 model steps issued two or more tool calls together, mostly groups of `view_file` and groups of `write_to_file`. #866 already calls these "parallel `run_command` invocations"; measured, they are sequential.

**Design.** An executor that classifies each tool call by its effect before running it, builds the dependency graph for the step, and runs independent calls on a bounded worker pool:

- read-only calls (`view_file`, `grep_search`, `list_dir`, `find_by_name`, `view_code_item`) never conflict with each other;
- write calls (`write_to_file`, `replace_file_content`) conflict only on the same path, so a per-path lock orders them and nothing else waits;
- `run_command` is opaque, so it runs concurrently with reads but takes a workspace-level write lock unless the model declares the paths it touches (a field the tool schema could gain);
- results are delivered to the transcript in issue order so the model sees what it expects, while execution order is free.

The subagent batching in #1220 is the same primitive one level up. A flag to keep today's serial behaviour (`--serial-tools`) covers tools with hidden side effects.

### 2. Two separate cache costs: full-context misses mid-run, and compaction resets

From the `usage` field of every `agent_response` step in 15 headless logs (1,279 model calls):

```text
all model calls:        uncached input 10,619,129    cache_read 192,374,637
17 calls with input > 100k and cache_read 0:   sum 3,292,077   = 31.0 % of all uncached input
```

The 17 calls: 235,586 · 138,825 · 142,623 · 211,798 · 268,032 · 114,335 · 190,518 · 203,716 · 256,725 · 199,481 · 226,232 · 220,215 · 208,848 · 113,735 · 169,938 · 181,072 · 210,398 tokens. Three are the first call of a resumed conversation (`agy -c`), which is a cold start and expected. The other 14 happened mid-run, in a conversation that was otherwise reading 235k–267k tokens from cache per call. 15 of the 17 came within two steps of a `system_message` step (subagent completion or scheduled wake), but 160 other `system_message` steps did not produce one, so that is where the miss shows, not proof of why. Several followed long tool waits (`run_command` of 551, 837 and 1,190 s). Nothing in the stream tells the user a miss happened; it is only visible by reading `cache_read_tokens`.

Compaction is a separate cost. 22 `checkpoint` steps in the same logs:

```text
durations (s): 35 39 41 42 43 44 45 55 60 60 62 78 90 109 116 134 135 136 147 151 224 602    median 70
checkpoint step usage: none reported
next call:  input 44,990–70,041   cache_read 0
following:  input ~3k            cache_read ~45–70k   (cache rebuilt from the new, shorter prefix)
```

So each compaction costs a minute or more of wall time during which nothing else happens, the summary call's tokens are not reported anywhere, and the prompt cache that had been serving ~98 % of each call is rebuilt from zero. #1245 reports the ~256k client-side cap and the cache invalidation; the thread there also shows a "mid-run prefix miss" of 243k tokens, which matches the 14 misses above.

The documentation for the model API says implicit caching is on by default and that hits are not guaranteed, and that explicit caching is not supported for Gemini 4 Argon and onward. So for the CLI's main model, the whole caching story is a best-effort prefix match, and the client has no handle it can hold.

**Design.**

- A byte-stable prefix contract inside the client: system prompt, tool declarations, customisations and history are appended only; nothing earlier in the request is rewritten between calls (no re-rendered timestamps, no re-ordered tool lists, no mutable "current state" block near the top). If any such mutation exists today, it is the first thing to look for behind the 14 misses.
- Miss telemetry: when a call's `cache_read_tokens` drops to zero while input exceeds the minimum, emit a `cache_miss` event in stream-json with the prefix hash of the previous call and this one, so users and the team can see what changed.
- Compaction as a cache-aware operation: run the summary request against the same prefix as the last call (so it is itself a cache hit rather than a fresh 250k read), report its usage in the checkpoint step, and do it in the background while the next model call is prepared, instead of a 70-second stop.
- At the API level, since the CLI and the model are the same company's: an explicit cache handle for Argon, or a request-level "reuse the prefix from request X" token, so a long run holds its context instead of hoping for an implicit hit.

### 3. Each headless invocation carries about 12 s of client-side overhead

Five runs of a one-token answer, wall clock from the shell against `duration_seconds` in the result JSON:

```text
agy -p "Reply with the single word OK." --model gemini-3.8-flash-low --output-format json
            wall    server   overhead   input    cache_read
yesterday   29.0    17.2     11.8       32,593   0          (cold prefix)
yesterday   16.0     4.7     11.3        4,021   28,577
today       16.7     4.5     12.2        4,014   28,577
today       17.1     5.0     12.1        4,020   28,577
today       19.8     8.2     11.6        4,019   28,577
```

The 32.6k-token prefix (rules, skills, tool declarations) is cached after the first call; the overhead is not. 11–12 s of start-up and shutdown is in the client, a 201 MB binary; what it does in those seconds (loading customisations, opening the summary store, the update check it performs) is not instrumented, so I cannot say which part dominates. #945 found the interactive TUI holding 0.8 of a core per turn and headless 0.03; this is the headless side of that question.

**Design.** A resident supervisor process (#749 asks for daemon mode) that holds the loaded customisations, tool schema, auth session and summary store open, with `agy -p` as a thin client over a local socket. Start-up work happens once per machine session, not once per prompt. An `agy --timing` flag that prints the start-up phases would let people report where the 12 s goes on their machine and would show the gain.

### 4. The Hub summary store is serialised whole, about every 1.5 s, while a run is active

While a long run was active I polled the file's mtime and size for 90 s:

```text
~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/jetbox_summaries_proto.pb   943 KB
27 rewrites in 90 s   gaps (s): 1.0 1.0 2.9 2.1 1.0 1.1 1.1 7.8 1.0 1.1 3.9 4.1 6.0 1.9 10.0 13.0 ...   median 1.5
size between rewrites: 943,232 → 943,235 → 943,238 → 943,241 → 943,238 bytes
```

The whole protobuf is re-serialised and swapped (`.pb.<uuid>.tmp`, then rename) to record changes of a few bytes. On a full disk (#1290) the same loop logged `[Hub Summaries] failed to write summaries file in persist` 152 times in 17 minutes. Next to it sits `conversation_summaries.db`, a SQLite database already in WAL mode, which is the right shape for this data.

For context, the desktop app's companion process on the same machine today: `language_server.exe` working set 12.96 GB, private 14.62 GB, running since 17 October; `agy.exe` 2.47 GB during a run. #727 (the `/resume` RAM spike) was marked resolved in a later release; this is a different process, and I note it only because it shares the machine with every CLI run.

**Design.** Make the summary store a journal: append one record per changed conversation, compact the journal on start-up or when it exceeds a size, and debounce persistence (coalesce changes within a window, write only when something changed). Or drop the protobuf and keep the summaries in the SQLite database that already exists beside it. Either way the write cost becomes proportional to the change, not to the size of the store.

### 5. CPU instruction use is fixed at build time instead of dispatched at run time

#378 (open since June, 13 comments, Core 2 and `kvm64` virtual CPUs) shows the installer dying with:

```text
FATAL ERROR: This binary was compiled with pclmul enabled, but this feature is not available on this processor (go/sigill-fail-fast).
Illegal instruction     "$BINARY_PATH" install
```

The message itself names the mechanism: the build enabled `PCLMULQDQ` unconditionally, and a fail-fast check at start-up refuses to run without it. The first comment on #378 attributes it to the BoringCrypto (FIPS) build of the Go toolchain; #605 asks for a workaround, and the only one in either thread is `qemu-x86_64 -cpu Haswell`.

This is the wrong layer to fix a CPU feature at. Go's own standard library already does it right: in `crypto/internal/fips140/aes/gcm/gcm_asm.go` the fast path is gated by `cpu.X86HasAES && cpu.X86HasPCLMULQDQ && cpu.X86HasSSE41 && cpu.X86HasSSSE3`, falls back to `sealGeneric` / `openGeneric` when the bits are absent, and even panics in tests if the generic path runs where hardware support exists. The fast instruction is used wherever the CPU has it and nowhere else, with one binary.

**Design.**

- Build the release at the x86-64 baseline (no compile-time `pclmul`, `aes` or AVX requirement) and keep every accelerated path behind a `cpuid` check with a portable fallback, which is what the Go runtime and BoringSSL's own capability vector are built to do. Speed stays where the hardware has it; the crash goes away where it does not.
- A CI job that boots the release binary under `qemu-x86_64 -cpu core2duo` and `-cpu kvm64` and runs `agy --version` and `agy install`, so the regression cannot ship again.
- Print the CPU feature set the binary expects in `agy doctor`, so a user on a hypervisor with a conservative CPU model gets a sentence instead of a `SIGILL`.

### What I did not measure

Why the 14 mid-run misses happened (the client does not expose what changed in the request); what the compaction summary call costs (its usage is not reported); whether the serial tool execution is in the executor or in the transport. The CLI has no reason to use the GPU, so this issue does not ask for that. I have the stream-json logs behind every number and can share them privately.

---

### Appendix D. How the numbers in sections 1–2 were computed

Run this against any `--output-format stream-json` log. It needs nothing but Python.

```python
import json, sys
rows = []
for line in open(sys.argv[1], encoding="utf-8", errors="ignore"):
    try: e = json.loads(line)
    except ValueError: continue
    su = e.get("step_update")
    if su and su.get("state") == "DONE":
        u = su.get("usage") or {}
        rows.append((su["step_index"], su["step_type"], su.get("tool_name"),
                     u.get("input_tokens") or 0, u.get("cache_read_tokens") or 0,
                     su.get("duration_seconds") or 0))
calls = [r for r in rows if r[1] == "agent_response"]
misses = [r for r in calls if r[3] > 100_000 and r[4] == 0]
ckpts = [r for r in rows if r[1] == "checkpoint"]
print("model calls", len(calls), "uncached input", sum(r[3] for r in calls),
      "cache_read", sum(r[4] for r in calls))
print("full-context misses", len(misses), "tokens", sum(r[3] for r in misses))
print("checkpoints", len(ckpts), "seconds", sorted(round(r[5]) for r in ckpts))
multi = 0; k = 0; seq = [r[1] for r in rows]
while k < len(seq):
    if seq[k] == "agent_response":
        j = k + 1
        while j < len(seq) and seq[j] == "tool": j += 1
        multi += (j - k - 1) >= 2; k = j
    else: k += 1
print("steps issuing 2+ tool calls", multi)
```

The summary-store cadence in section 4 was measured by polling `os.stat()` of `jetbox_summaries_proto.pb` four times a second for 90 s and recording every change of `st_mtime_ns` or size. The headless overhead in section 3 is `time.time()` around `subprocess.run([...])` minus `duration_seconds` from the result JSON.
